newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan N-activists gather for nuclear waste ship.
newsitem.headline: Japan N-activists gather for nuclear waste ship.

text.p: Anti-nuclear activists gathered in northern Japan on Sunday to protest against the arrival of a British ship carrying nuclear waste, a week after Japan's worst nuclear accident.

The Pacific Teal, which left the French port of Cherbourg on January 13 carrying waste processed in France, is scheduled to arrive on Tuesday at Mutsu-Ogawara in Aomori Prefecture, about 580 km (360 miles) northeast of Tokyo.
Activists said they plan rallies early Tuesday morning at the placid northern Japanese port which was custom-built to handle a series of nuclear-waste shipments.
Greenpeace Japan had planned to send a ship to stop the Pacific Teal from entering port, but abandoned the plan when the owner of the boat refused to lend his craft at the last minute.
"But we have other plans. We may be able to find our way out into the sea," Greenpeace spokeswoman Noriko Oyama told Reuters.
The waste initially came from Japan and was processed under a deal between the French state company COGEMA (Compagnie Generale des Matieres Nucleaires) and 10 Japanese power firms.
It includes radioactive material such as strontium, which has a half-life of several million years. The waste is mixed with glass and encased in 40 stainless steel cannisters.

After testing for radioactivity leakage, the cannisters will be stored for 30 to 50 years at a special cooling facility at nearby Rokkasho village, Japan's only storage facility, and later buried at an unspecified location.
The government has not selected the waste's end destination and residents fear they may be stuck with the toxic material.

When a first shipment arrived in 1995, Aomori authorities refused entry at the last minute until the central government promised in a written statement not to seek permanent burial of the toxic waste in the prefecture.
Local authorities say last week's explosion at a nuclear reprocessing facility in Tokaimura has increased residents' concern.
"That was a nasty accident at a nasty time," Rokkasho village chief Hiroshi Tsushida said after the accident.

A fire which caused radiation to escape at the Tokaimuira facility, 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo, was not extinguished properly and caused an explosion hours later, exposing 37 workers to radiation.

Investigation of the accident has so far revealed startling lapses in safety standards including outdated firefighting equipment and delays in alerting both local residents and central authorities of the crisis.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who was not informed of the accident for several hours, formally apologised to the nation in parliament for the lapses.

Since the Tokaimura incident two other nuclear plants, part of a 50-plant network that supply one-third of Japan's power needs, have either shut or cut back production because of maintenance checks that found flaws in their operations.
Under the terms of an agreement between Japan, Britain and France, spent Japanese uranium fuel is reprocessed into plutonium and the waste produced stored in Japan.
Tokyo plans eventually to ship 7,100 tonnes of spent fuel to France and Britain for reprocessing into 30 tonnes of fuel-grade plutonium, yielding 3,000 tonnes of waste.
Japanese authorities plan to move to plutonium technology to boost its self-sufficiency in energy needs to more than 50 per cent by the early 21st century.
